title: Use population data

blocks.heading: Use population data
blocks.text: Population data can guide the location and capacity of services, employment planning and infrastructure. For a Namibian planning application, compare district age groups and access to schools or clinics rather than distributing capacity solely by national totals. Use the date and local denominators.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Economic uses
blocks.text:
Age and location data can inform workforce training, transport demand and markets. Counts of working-age residents do not directly measure available skills or job seekers; combine population structure with relevant labour information.

Applied example: Age and working-age numbers help plan future training and labour needs. The size and location of households help estimate demand for goods and services.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Social uses
blocks.text:
Children’s and older residents’ counts can inform school, health and care planning. Needs depend on location and actual access as well as age. A distant facility may offer less usable capacity than its place count suggests.

Applied example: Child population estimates help plan school places. The number and location of older residents help plan accessible health and support services.

blocks.heading: Apply the measure
blocks.text: A fictional district expects 360 children to need primary places and currently has 240 usable places, a gap of 120. A neighbouring district expects 180 children and has 200 places. The first has the larger capacity gap, but staff, classroom condition and journey distances still matter. A total population count alone would not reveal this age-specific need.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Match data to a planning decision
blocks.text: Age and working-age numbers help estimate future training and labour needs. Household totals and locations help judge demand for goods and services. Child numbers support planning for school places; the location and number of older people support planning for accessible care. Use a relevant area and period and check denominators: a count of people can grow even when their percentage share falls.
